thesisInOneSentence: MELT lets a transformer 'think' for more internal loops without paying for those loops in KV-cache memory, by replacing the append-only cache with a single per-layer cache whose contents are gated forward across iterations.
audience: Engineers and researchers comfortable with attention and KV caches; may have heard of looped transformers but does not need to have read the Ouro paper.
hook: Reasoning models like Ouro think harder by looping their own layers — but every loop bloats the KV cache linearly. MELT shows you can decouple the two.

teaser.openingLine: Reasoning models pay a hidden tax — every extra step of 'thinking' triples your KV cache. MELT just stopped paying it.
teaser.stakes: On a 32k-token generation, Ouro burns about 28 GB of VRAM; MELT does the same iterative reasoning in under 10 GB — roughly Qwen-size memory with looped-model accuracy.
teaser.openLoop: How can a model loop its layers four times and somehow keep one KV cache the same size as a non-looped model — without the accuracy collapsing?
teaser.visualConcept: Two stacked bars animate side-by-side: Ouro's KV cache grows row by row with each loop until it dwarfs the model weights; MELT's cache stays as a single rewritten row. Title 'MELT: Memory-Efficient Looped Transformer' lands AT THE END as the payoff.

narrativeArc.name: Teaser
narrativeArc.purpose: Cold-open hook → stakes (28 GB → 10 GB at 32k) → open-loop question (how can looping not grow memory?) → title card lands as the payoff. 5-7 micro-beats, no equations, no jargon beyond 'KV cache'.

narrativeArc.name: The hidden cost of thinking longer
narrativeArc.purpose: Frame the broader landscape: chain-of-thought scales reasoning horizontally (more output tokens) while latent reasoning (looped transformers like Ouro) scales it vertically (more internal compute). Both let you 'think longer' — but both have a memory cost the user doesn't see. Set up that vertical reasoning's cost lives in the KV cache.

narrativeArc.name: What a looped transformer actually does
narrativeArc.purpose: Quick refresher on looped transformers: same N layers, T iterations. Show the F^(T) composition; emphasize 'same parameters, more compute'. Lead viewer to the question: where do those T iterations land in memory? Land on: every loop appends a fresh row to the KV cache at each layer, so memory ~ N × L × T.

narrativeArc.name: The bottleneck made concrete
narrativeArc.purpose: Make the scaling visceral. For a 32k-token generation: Ouro = 25.17 GB of KV cache alone, vs 3.67 GB for Qwen, vs MELT's 6.29 GB. Show that for long reasoning the KV cache dwarfs the model weights themselves. This is why you can't naively scale loop count T.

narrativeArc.name: MELT's idea: rewrite, don't append
narrativeArc.purpose: Core architectural pivot. Per layer, keep ONE KV cache that all T loops share. Each loop updates a latent state h_t via a learnable gate z_t (sigmoid of an affine function of x_t and h_{t-1}). New state = z ⊙ old + (1-z) ⊙ new — a GRU-style convex combination. Then project h_t through W_K, W_V to get the single K, V row for this token at this layer, reused across loops. Use the metaphor: working memory rewritten in place vs scratchpad that grows. Briefly note the ablation: naive 'last loop only' or 'mean' fails — the learned gate is doing real work.

narrativeArc.name: Training MELT without breaking it
narrativeArc.purpose: Two engineering bits, fast. (i) Chunk-wise training: MELT's per-token KV update is sequential across tokens, so you can't do full-sequence parallel SFT; chunks balance fidelity vs throughput. (ii) Two-phase fine-tuning from a pretrained Ouro: Phase 1 interpolates KV = α·KV_MELT + (1-α)·KV_base with α growing 0→1 (smooth transition); Phase 2 freezes Ouro as teacher and adds an attention-aligned distillation loss across every layer × every loop. Ablation hammer: remove chunk-wise training → 0% accuracy on every math benchmark. The recipe is the paper, not just the architecture.

narrativeArc.name: Does it actually work?
narrativeArc.purpose: Headline numbers, honestly. MELT-1.6B beats every same-size standard transformer baseline (Qwen3-1.7B, Gemma4-E2B, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B) on most benchmarks, with KV memory ~4× smaller than Ouro and only ~1.7× larger than Qwen. It's slightly behind Ouro on the hardest math sets — Ouro keeps 4× more KV per token. Figure 1a (memory-vs-accuracy scatter) is the picture that lands the trade-off.

narrativeArc.name: Limits and what's next
narrativeArc.purpose: Three honest caveats, fast: loop count T is fixed at inference (no adaptive depth yet); MELT doesn't use MQA, so the gap with Qwen on memory could close further; training is still sequential across tokens, limiting parallelism.

narrativeArc.name: Closing
narrativeArc.purpose: One-sentence framing + title card. Scaling language models used to mean making them bigger or making them talk longer; MELT lets them think longer inside their own hidden state, at fixed memory. End on paper title + arXiv link.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: establishes the baseline architecture being modified — same N layers re-applied T times
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers conflate 'looped' with 'recurrent' (RNN-style across tokens); here it's recurrent across iterations of the same layer stack on the same hidden states
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — show N layers as a vertical stack, then unroll T copies side by side; emphasize SAME weights θ_1..θ_N reused. End on F^(T) composition equation.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: this is the entire bottleneck MELT attacks; memory ~ N × L × T grows with reasoning depth
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers think KV cache only grows with sequence length L; in looped models it also grows with depth T (multiplicative, not additive)
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — build a 3D grid (layer × token × loop) of KV entries; rotate to show how T inflates a 2D grid into a 3D box. Show concrete number: 32k tokens, 4 loops → 25 GB.

conceptsToVisualize.concept: MELT's single shared KV cache per layer
conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: the structural contrast with looped baselines: one K, V row per token per layer total, reused across all T loops
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers may think MELT skips loops or shares across layers (it does neither — same N layers, same T loops, but the cache is rewritten in place)
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — side-by-side: Ouro grows a stack of T KV rows per token across loops; MELT keeps a single KV row that gets *rewritten* by the gate each loop. The total cache for MELT collapses from O(N×L×T) → O(N×L).

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: this is the actual mechanism that lets one KV row carry information across loops without forgetting prior iterations
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers may not know GRU-style gates; many will assume MELT just averages or takes the last loop. Ablation in the paper shows mean/EMA/last are all dramatically worse.
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — derivation in 3 steps. (1) Show z_t as sigmoid(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z). (2) Visualize h_t = z ⊙ h_{t-1} + (1-z) ⊙ x_t as a per-dimension mix dial: z→1 means 'keep old', z→0 means 'take new'. (3) Project h_t through W_K, W_V to get the single k_t, v_t row. Use contour highlight on z and (1-z) when the voice names them.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: shows that the rest of the transformer block is unchanged — only the K, V production pathway is modified
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers may think MELT changes attention itself; it doesn't, only the way k_t and v_t are produced from h_t
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — highlight the standard residual attention + FFN block, and dim everything except the K/V production arrow which now flows through the latent state h_t.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: KV = α·KV_MELT + (1-α)·KV_base with α: 0→1 — this is what lets MELT inherit Ouro's pretrained knowledge instead of training from scratch
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers may not see why a sudden architectural swap fails; the paper's Table 4 shows direct transition drops accuracy ~9 points on AIME24 pass@1
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — two parallel KV computations (orange LoopLM stream, pink MELT stream) blend through a moving slider α from 0 to 1 over training steps. Reference Figure 3b directly.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: Phase 2 keeps MELT representations from drifting from the frozen LoopLM teacher; ablation shows removing it costs ~2 pass@1 points on AIME24
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: viewers conflate KD on output logits with activation-level distillation; this aligns post-attention outputs at every layer × every loop
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — show the loss as a sum over an N × T grid where each cell measures ‖o_MELT − sg(o_LoopLM)‖² at that layer and loop. The grid lights up as alignment is enforced.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: the empirical claim: MELT sits in a previously empty region of the plot — non-looped memory budget, looped-model accuracy
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: without the plot, viewers can't appreciate how clean the separation is
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: paper page spotlight on Figure 1a. NOTE: the figure's y-axis is AIME26 pass@1 in the actual image (the paper's caption mentioning MATH-500 is mismatched). Then a Manim re-animation: dots for Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek, MELT (highlighted), Ouro — draw the line that MELT is the closest to the top-left.

Where does a KV cache live, and why does it grow with reasoning depth?

derivationsToBuild.concept: KV-cache memory scaling: O(N×L) vs O(N×L×T)
derivationsToBuild.openingQuestion: Where exactly does the KV cache grow when you loop?
stepsToShow: Show a single transformer block computing K, V for one token at one layer — one row added
Stack N layers — cache grows to N rows per token, total ~ O(N×L)
Now loop the stack T times — each loop appends a fresh row per layer per token, total ~ O(N×L×T)
Concretize with the paper's numbers: 32k tokens, Ouro = 25.17 GB KV cache vs Qwen = 3.67 GB
MELT's collapse: keep ONE row per token per layer, regardless of T — total back to O(N×L), measured 6.29 GB

derivationsToBuild.concept: the gated update as convex combination
derivationsToBuild.openingQuestion: If you only keep one cache, how does it remember loop 1 by the time you're at loop 4?
stepsToShow: Show the gate z_t = σ(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z) — a vector of per-dimension dials between 0 and 1
Show h_t = z ⊙ h_{t-1} + (1 - z) ⊙ x_t — per-dimension convex combination
Two limit cases: z→1 (keep old state, ignore new input) and z→0 (overwrite with new input)
Brief: paper ablates naive 'last loop only' and 'mean of all loops' — both drop ~10+ points on AIME24, so the learned gate is doing real work
Plug h_t into k_t = h_t W_K, v_t = h_t W_V — the single K, V row everyone attends to

derivationsToBuild.concept: interpolated transition: α-fade from LoopLM to MELT
derivationsToBuild.openingQuestion: Why can't you just swap the architecture and keep training?
stepsToShow: Show two parallel KV streams: KV_base (vanilla LoopLM forward) and KV_MELT (the new gated path)
Animate α from 0 to 1 over training steps — model smoothly inherits LoopLM behavior, then drifts toward MELT
Land on: without this fade, ablation drops AIME24 pass@1 by ~9 points

metaphors.concept: MELT's single shared KV cache vs Ouro's per-loop cache
metaphors.metaphor: A scratchpad you keep erasing and rewriting in place vs a scratchpad where you take a fresh sheet for every step of work and never throw any of them out. Both let you reason for many steps; only one fits in your pocket.
metaphors.whenToDeploy: act-4 opening, right after revealing the architectural pivot — lands the 'rewrite vs append' intuition before any math

metaphors.concept: the gated update z ⊙ h + (1-z) ⊙ x
metaphors.metaphor: A mixing board with one slider per latent dimension: at z=1 you hold the old recording; at z=0 you patch in the new take; in between you crossfade. The network learns the slider positions per dimension and per token.
metaphors.whenToDeploy: act-4, when introducing the gate — pairs with the Manim of dials moving

metaphors.metaphor: Crossfading from one song into another instead of cutting abruptly between tracks. The model is the DJ; α is the fader.
metaphors.whenToDeploy: act-5, when introducing Phase 1 — explains why a sudden architectural swap fails

narrativeAngles: Frame the entire video around decoupling compute from memory. These have been one knob in transformers for years (bigger models = more of both); MELT is a clean wedge that separates them.
Frame MELT as 'GRU dynamics smuggled into transformer KV caches' — the gate equation IS the GRU update rule, applied to a per-token latent state per layer.
Frame the training recipe as the real innovation: the architecture is clean but doesn't train without the chunk-wise + two-phase recipe (ablation: remove chunk-wise → 0.0 accuracy across the board).
criticisms: The paper does NOT clearly disentangle how much of the win comes from MELT's architecture vs. the two-phase fine-tuning from a powerful Ouro teacher. The 'MELT outperforms standard LLMs' claim is conditional on Ouro pretraining — would MELT trained from scratch even work? Not answered.
Figure 1a's caption says 'MATH-500 accuracy versus memory' but the actual figure on page 1 shows AIME26 pass@1 on the y-axis. We must reference what the figure shows, not the caption.

Memory comparison glosses over that Qwen3-1.7B (3.67 GB KV at 32k) is still ~1.7× cheaper than MELT (6.29 GB). The paper attributes this to MELT not yet using MQA; we should be honest that MELT's memory is 'comparable' not 'equal' to standard LLMs.
The arXiv ID format '2605.07721' implies May 2026 — verify the cite resolves at recording time; if not, refer to the paper by title.
Code release is promised ('will be released soon') but not yet available. Mention only if asked; don't dwell.

We MUST derive (not state) why a naive 'just keep one KV row' fails — the ablation shows mean/EMA/last variants drop ~15 points on AIME24 vs full MELT. The gate is doing real work, and viewers need to feel that.
